title: US Prepares For Possible Strikes, Midterm Early Voting, Trump BBC Deposition
description_html:
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as oil prices climb and the prospect of another attack on Iran grows.
More than 19 million Americans have already voted, with strong turnout among Democrats and voters of color, but the numbers can’t tell us who will win.
A judge has ordered President Trump to testify in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC, potentially forcing him to answer questions about his finances and January 6.

Want more analysis of the most important news of the day, plus a little fun? Subscribe to the Up First newsletter.

Support public media with NPR+ and enjoy perks for over 25 podcasts like this one. This show’s perks include sponsor-free listening. Learn more at plus.npr.org.

Today’s episode of Up First was edited by Andrew Sussman, Megan Pratz, Emily Kopp, Mohamad ElBardicy and Alice Woelfle.

It was produced by Iman Maani and Nia Dumas.

Our director is Christopher Thomas.

We get engineering support from Neisha Heinis.

Our technical director is Zac Coleman.

And our Executive Producer is Jay Shaylor.

(1:53) U.S. Iran War
(5:38) Early Voting
(9:08) Trump vs. BBC Deposition

cues.t: The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East.
Oil prices are climbing back up as signs point to a possible military attack on Iran.
What could another round of fighting accomplish?
I'm Leila Fadel.
That's A Martínez, and this is UP FIRST from NPR News.
Almost 21 million people have already voted.
Turnout is way up in key battleground states compared to the last midterms.
What can we learn from the data?
And President Trump will have to testify in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
A judge said if he wants to sue, he has to play by the court's rules.
What could the BBC ask the president under oath?
Stay with us.
We got the news you need to start your day.
There are tangible moves that point to the possibility of more heavy fighting in Iran in the next few weeks.
Military reinforcements are moving in, and some U.S. personnel are moving out of the region.
To break this all down, we're joined by NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre.

So, Greg, we heard yesterday about the potential plans between the U.S. and Israel maybe to launch a major strike or major strikes from someone who was briefed on them and talked to NPR on the condition of anonymity.
What more do we know today?
Yeah, a few bits and pieces.
But perhaps the only person who knows for sure what will happen is President Trump, and he's being intentionally vague.
And as we've seen previously in this war, Trump often changes his mind.
The U.S. military will prepare for one possible action only to have it called off by Trump, and he'll go in a different direction.
What we do have are clear signs of preparations for a possible attack.
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a low-key visit to Israel this week, where he met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Some U.S. State Department officials and family members are moving out of Saudi Arabia.
So collectively, this points to the growing possibility, but not the certainty, of military action.
OK.
So if there was going to be action, would it be before or after the November 3 midterm elections?
Yeah, A, it seems much more likely afterward.
Trump wants lower oil prices, and military action is going to cause the price to jump.
In fact, today, Brent crude oil is trading at $114 a barrel - this is the highest since May - just based on the talk of possible action.
Israel has elections on Tuesday, and Netanyahu is battling for his political survival.
This is another complicating factor.
And the U.S. military pieces aren't all in place.
That third U.S. aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, won't be in the region for another week or so.
All right.
How is Iran preparing for the possibility of more fighting?
So Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said yesterday that his country was prepared for both diplomacy and war.
Iran continues to fire on oil tankers going through the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran claimed Thursday that seven were hit.
Now, Trump pushed back, saying this just wasn't true; it was just an attempt to drive up oil prices.
Now, Iran says it could also target a range of facilities in Arab Gulf States.
And as we know, Iranian missiles and drones have hit key oil and gas hubs, airports, commercial areas and have caused significant damage.
Iran would also try to attack U.S. military bases and ships.
And we've seen recently these damage reports by the U.S. government that are much higher than the Pentagon originally let on - that Iran hit 81 planes and more than a dozen U.S. military bases.
I guess the largest overall question is would more fighting end the war?
It's just impossible to predict if this round would be different than the previous ones.
The U.S. and Israel still have the firepower to inflict additional heavy damage.
But there's been no sign that Iran is on the verge of making major concessions - really, to the contrary.
Iran is making demands.
It wants formal control over the Strait of Hormuz.
It wants U.S. troops out of the region.
For the U.S., there are two critical issues that haven't changed since the early days of the war - a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a deal on Iran's nuclear program.
All right.
That's NPR's Greg Myre.
Greg, thanks a lot.
Sure thing, A.
The latest data this morning shows almost 21 million people have cast their votes in the midterms.
Yeah.
That's according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, which tracks those numbers.
The early-voting figure is a combination of voting by mail and in person.
NPR politics reporter Saige Miller is here.
Saige, 21 million seems like a lot of votes to cast so far.
I mean, how does that compare to past years?
It is a lot of votes so far, and it's up about 2 million just since yesterday.
And in key battleground states, early voting is up significantly compared to the last midterm election.
In the 2022 midterms, nearly 122 million people voted.
So 21 million now is a big slice of that.
And so I called up Michael McDonald.
He's a political science professor at the University of Florida, and he also maintains the university's Election Lab data on early voting.
And he says voter participation is looking pretty solid.
When I look on a state-by-state basis, what I see is turnout is up over the 2022 and 2018 midterm elections.
And keep in mind, 2018 was the highest turnout rate for a midterm election since 1914.
All right, so he's saying turnout is up.
But what can we glean so far from this election - from the early-voting numbers we have?
It's important not to over-interpret early-voting data because it's often a poor predictor of final results.
But McDonald says there are certain kinds of voters who are hitting the polls sooner than others.
In states that have detailed data, Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans.
That could be attributed to Democratic enthusiasm.
And we've seen supercharged Democratic turnout in most of the elections since President Trump took office.
But Democrats aren't the only voting group voting early.
It's up among unaffiliated voters.
And in states like North Carolina and Georgia, McDonald says voters of color are showing up in droves.
African American turnout is up.
Hispanics have more than doubled their performance at the same day in 2022.

Even though Republicans aren't voting at the same rate as Democrats, it doesn't mean that they're sitting this one out, A. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to vote on Election Day.
That's what's happened in the last few elections, and there's no reason to think it'll be any different this time.
What about in some of the competitive races?
What can we tell about early voting in those races?
OK.
Let's look at Texas again, where there's a competitive Senate race in red Texas.
McDonald says the numbers show people are activated.
As of yesterday, there was over half a million more people who had voted than in 2022, a 50% increase of early voting.
I do want to stress, even though we know people are motivated to vote, we don't know how they're voting.

But Trump knows this is a tough environment for Republicans, so he's doing what he can to encourage they show up, like traveling all over the country to support Republicans on the ballot in an attempt to energize voters.
We also don't know and have zero way to tell if turnout will be high on Election Day and if Republicans will make up for that early voting gap.
We will all just have to wait until November 3 to solve that mystery.
All right.
That's NPR politics reporter Saige Miller. Saige, thanks.
Thank you.
President Trump will have to sit for a deposition in a $10 billion defamation case he brought against the BBC.
Yeah.
A federal magistrate judge ruled Thursday that it was Trump's choice to sue the British broadcaster, and he has to play by the rules of the court or face sanctions.
NPR media correspondent David Folkenflik attended the hearing in Miami.
David, why was there even a question about whether the president would sit for a deposition?
Well, I mean, he is the president.
And it's this president - right, A?
You know, this was a - in some ways, a hearing about logistics in front of a magistrate judge.

It sounds like it's a pretty pro forma kind of thing, but actually, you know, really fundamentally at its core is a question of whether the sitting president of the United States will submit to the will of a federal court.
He had agreed to sit for a deposition, which is to say questions under oath, for last Friday, October 16, but it was canceled.
President's legal team said it was due to matters of national importance and said he could do it sometime in January.
There's a deadline in mid-December for the completion of what's called discovery.
It's where the two sides get evidence from one another for this case.
Trump's private attorney invoked the idea yesterday the president does a lot more things than you could possibly know.
The BBC's lead attorney said, hey, that's fake news.
He noted that last Friday, Trump campaigned with a Republican Senate candidate in Dalton, Georgia, then went to Mar-a-Lago for an event for the Republican National Committee.
The magistrate judge said, no. Let's do this.
You're going to have to do this by December 11.
Discovery is supposed to wrap up by a week later.
There's a possibility that could shift if the judge presiding over the case changes the deadline.
And the judge also said, look; you got to hand over evidence.

All the material that the president's legal team - he's suing as a private individual - gave to the BBC was stuff that the BBC had either handed over to the president's team or that - stuff that the president's legal team, according to the BBC's lawyers, had pulled down from the internet - not any private records at all.
The judge said that strained credulity that there were not more records that were - needed to be given over that were responsive for the BBC's case.
All right, so tell us about the case.

So back in October of 2024, just a few weeks before the presidential elections, the BBC show "Panorama" broadcast a documentary in which it spliced together parts of the January 6 speech, 2021, that made it seem as though Trump, at that, you know, pivotal day when there was a siege of Congress - made it seem like he was bluntly calling for violence to prevent the certification of Joe Biden as the winner of that race.
Trump said this was false, deceptive and defamatory under Florida law - is seeking $10 billion.
He's tweaked a little bit the grounds on which he's doing it, putting aside the claim that he made initially that this damaged his business and future financial prospects.
Now he's talking mostly about his reputational injury.
But as the BBC argues, his reputation is bound up in business and politics.

I want to point out to listeners, "Panorama" was not aired in Florida or on U.S. channels or on the BBC's, you know, streaming partners here in the U.S. And the other thing the BBC points out is Trump not only won the 2024 race.
He won Florida, handily, too.
What's the BBC hope to learn from Trump's testimony?
Well, it's making the argument that if there's a harm to his business or Mar-a-Lago, that might undermine the case he was damaged.
The BBC did apologize for the splicing.
It did - in fact, there was a fallout for some of its officials.
But it's now trying to determine what his mindset was.
Maybe they can show that he did want to encourage violence.
They noted that a lot of defendants said Trump's speech had urged them on.
Last thing, David.
I mean, President Trump has sued lots of news organizations.
What's the significance of this one?
So at the outset of President Trump's term, media outlets were settling.
That is, you saw ABC and CBS settle lawsuits that President Trump had filed as a private citizen, trying to just kind of resolve it and get through.

And it doesn't seem to have stopped his onslaught of lawsuits against other news outlets or him sometimes having government agencies investigate them or go after them and their parent companies nonetheless.
So you've seen here the BBC fighting back legally.
It's really going after details of January 6.
The judges have made clear they don't want this to be completely relitigated, the question of what happened January 6, 2021.
And yet it's a key core element of this case.

They're looking at ways to show that Trump has actually profited since retaking the White House, not been damaged, undermining that $10 billion claim - also potentially going after another vulnerability of the president.

He doesn't really want his financial details public, and they are securing information about both the level of interest in people joining Mar-a-Lago, his resort, as members and what costs he has charged them over the years.There's - in addition, at the core question, if there's evidence that President Trump or people around him wanted to encourage violence on January 6, the president wouldn't want that public either.
So you're seeing the BBC fight.
And you're also seeing others battle back, as well, particularly if you look at ABC's case against the Federal Communications Commission over its TV licenses it holds.
And CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the White House, as well, over the questions of access.
Trump right now in this lawsuit has to decide how willing he is to play by the rules.
Is he willing to submit to the rule of law in federal court in a lawsuit that he voluntarily brought?
And if not, it looks very likely that this case will be dismissed.
That's NPR media correspondent David Folkenflik. David, thanks.
You bet.

study.one_liner_ko: 미국이 이란 추가 공습 가능성에 대비해 항공모함을 증파하는 가운데, 중간선거 사전투표가 약 2,100만 표에 달했고, 트럼프는 BBC 상대 100억 달러 명예훼손 소송에서 증언대에 서게 됐다.
summary_ko: 미국이 세 번째 항공모함을 중동에 보내고 일부 국무부 인력과 가족이 사우디를 떠나는 등, 이란 추가 공격 가능성을 보여주는 구체적 움직임이 나타났다. 다만 트럼프가 계획을 자주 바꾸고 의도적으로 모호하게 말하기 때문에 확정된 것은 없다.
공격은 11월 3일 중간선거 이후일 가능성이 더 크다. 트럼프는 유가 하락을 원하는데 군사행동은 유가를 올린다. 브렌트유는 이미 배럴당 114달러로 5월 이후 최고치다. 이란은 호르무즈 해협 통제권과 미군 철수를 요구하며 양보 기미가 없다.
플로리다대 선거 연구소 집계로 사전투표는 약 2,100만 표다. 주요 경합주에서 2022년 중간선거보다 크게 늘었다. 민주당, 무당층, 유색인종 유권자의 참여가 두드러진다.
사전투표 데이터는 최종 결과의 예측 지표로는 약하다. 공화당은 원래 선거 당일에 더 많이 투표하는 경향이 있어서, 격차가 메워질지는 11월 3일까지 알 수 없다.
연방 치안판사가 트럼프에게 12월 11일까지 BBC 소송의 증언 녹취(deposition)에 응하라고 명령했다. 소송을 직접 제기했으니 법원 규칙을 따라야 하고, 안 그러면 제재를 받는다는 취지다.
BBC '파노라마'가 1월 6일 연설을 편집해 폭력을 부추긴 것처럼 보이게 했다는 것이 소송의 핵심이다. BBC는 이 기회에 트럼프의 재산·마러라고 회원 정보와 1월 6일 관련 증거를 파고들 수 있다. 트럼프가 규칙을 거부하면 소송이 기각될 가능성이 크다.
study.summary_en: So, three big stories this morning. First, the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and there are real signs of another strike on Iran. But Trump keeps changing his mind, and any action looks more likely after the midterms, since he wants lower oil prices. Second, almost 21 million Americans have already voted, with Democrats and voters of color turning out strongly. Still, early voting is a poor predictor, and Republicans usually vote on Election Day. Third, a judge ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion BBC lawsuit. If he won't play by the court's rules, the case could be dismissed.

expressions.quote: he has to play by the rules of the court or face sanctions
expressions.nuance_ko: 공정성이나 절차를 따를 것을 요구할 때 쓴다. 'if you want X, you have to play by the rules'는 불평이나 경고의 뉘앙스로 자주 나온다. 규칙을 피해가는 상대를 비판할 때 'doesn't play by the rules'라고 한다.
examples: If you want the promotion, you've got to play by the rules like everyone else.
Some airlines just don't play by the rules when it comes to refunds.
I'm happy to negotiate, but we all have to play by the same rules.

similar.expression: follow the rules of the game
similar.example: Startups that disrupt a market still have to follow the rules of the game.
He'll toe the line for now, but he's clearly unhappy.

expressions.nuance_ko: 기자가 취재원 신원을 밝히지 않는 조건으로 정보를 받을 때 쓰는 뉴스 표현이다. 'spoke on condition of anonymity'로 the를 빼고도 쓴다. 일상에서는 농담조로 쓰기도 한다.
examples: Two employees told the paper, on the condition of anonymity, that layoffs were coming.
She shared the story with me on the condition of anonymity, so please don't name her.
I'll tell you what he said, but only on the condition of anonymity.

similar.example: Off the record, I think the merger is dead.
The official agreed to speak on background only.

expressions.quote: Iran is on the verge of making major concessions
expressions.nuance_ko: 뒤에 명사나 -ing가 온다. 좋은 일에도 나쁜 일에도 쓰고, 'on the brink of'보다 약간 덜 극적이다. 'on the verge of tears'는 정해진 표현이다.
examples: The team is on the verge of winning its first title in twenty years.
I was on the verge of quitting when my manager offered me a new role.
The restaurant is on the verge of closing after the rent hike.

similar.example: The two sides are on the brink of a deal.
I was about to call you.

expressions.nuance_ko: 앞 내용을 부정하며 반대 사실을 덧붙일 때 쓴다. 'no sign of X — quite to the contrary'처럼 말하면 논지가 선명해진다. 'evidence to the contrary(반대 증거)'도 자주 쓰는 형태다.
examples: People assumed he'd be upset, but, to the contrary, he seemed relieved.
There's no evidence the policy is working. Quite the contrary, prices are up.
Unless you hear to the contrary, we'll meet at six.

similar.example: I'm not annoyed. On the contrary, I'm impressed.
It didn't hurt sales. If anything, it helped.

expressions.expression: only to have it called off
expressions.quote: only to have it called off by Trump
expressions.nuance_ko: 'prepare/do X only to have Y happen' 구조로, 노력 뒤에 허탈한 반전이 온다는 뜻이다. 'call off'는 이미 계획된 것을 취소한다는 뜻의 구동사다. 뒤에 to부정사가 오는 'only to find/realize'도 같은 패턴이다.
examples: We booked the whole venue, only to have the event called off two days before.
She trained for months, only to have the race called off because of the weather.
I rushed to the airport, only to find the flight had been delayed.

similar.example: He drove two hours, only to find the shop was closed.
They scrapped the launch at the last minute.

expressions.quote: voters of color are showing up in droves
expressions.nuance_ko: 사람들이 대규모로 몰려가거나 떠나는 상황에 쓴다. 'leave in droves', 'flock in droves'가 흔하다. 보통 사람에게 쓰고 사물에는 거의 쓰지 않는다.
examples: Fans turned up in droves despite the rain.
Customers are leaving in droves since the price hike.
Young professionals are moving out of the city in droves.

similar.example: People came out in large numbers to protest.
Tourists flock to the old town every summer.

expressions.nuance_ko: 선거, 경기, 논쟁, 모임 등에 이번만 불참한다는 가벼운 뉘앙스다. 'I'll sit this one out'은 초대를 정중하게 거절할 때 유용하다. 영구 불참이 아니라 이번 한 번이라는 뜻이 들어 있다.
examples: I'm exhausted, so I think I'll sit this one out tonight.
A few big names are sitting this one out at the tournament.
You can sit this one out if you don't feel strongly about the issue.

similar.example: I'll pass on dinner, but thanks.
He stayed on the sidelines during the debate.

expressions.quote: Republicans will make up for that early voting gap
expressions.nuance_ko: 부족하거나 잃은 것을 다른 것으로 채운다는 뜻이다. 목적어에 갭, 실수, 손실, 시간이 자주 온다. 'make it up to someone'은 사람에게 보상한다는 별개 표현이다.
examples: We lost the morning, but we can make up for it by working late.
He tried to make up for missing the meeting by sending detailed notes.
Great service doesn't make up for cold food.

similar.example: Extra hours can't compensate for poor planning.
The challenger is trying to close the gap in the polls.

expressions.quote: his reputation is bound up in business and politics
expressions.nuance_ko: 두 가지를 떼어서 생각하기 어려울 때 쓰는 약간 격식 있는 표현이다. 논쟁에서 '이 둘은 분리할 수 없다'고 주장할 때 유용하다. 'bound up with'로도 쓴다.
examples: For many people, their identity is bound up in their job.
The city's history is bound up in the story of its port.
His mood is bound up with how the team is doing.

similar.example: Housing and health are inextricably linked.
Good sleep and good focus go hand in hand.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'It strains credulity that...'은 어떤 주장이 너무 비현실적이라 믿기 어렵다는 격식 있는 비판이다. 판사, 변호사, 칼럼니스트가 자주 쓴다. 회의에서 상대 주장을 정중하지만 날카롭게 반박할 때 쓸 수 있다.
examples: It strains credulity to say nobody noticed the error for a year.
His excuse for being late again really strains credulity.
The claim that sales tripled overnight strains credulity.

similar.example: That explanation is a bit hard to swallow.
The sheer waste of it beggars belief.

expressions.quote: really fundamentally at its core is a question of whether
expressions.nuance_ko: 표면적 논쟁을 넘어 진짜 쟁점을 짚을 때 쓴다. 'at its core, this is about X'는 논점 프레이밍에 매우 유용하다. 'at heart', 'fundamentally'와 비슷하다.
examples: At its core, this disagreement is about trust, not money.
The debate over remote work is, at its core, a debate about control.
At its core, good teamwork is just clear communication.

similar.expression: when it comes down to it
similar.example: When it comes down to it, we just need more time.
The bottom line is that we can't afford it.

expressions.quote: Trump pushed back, saying this just wasn't true
expressions.nuance_ko: 주장이나 요청에 정면으로 반대 의사를 밝힌다는 뜻이다. 직장에서 'I'll push back on that'은 정중하지만 단호한 반대로 들린다. 명사형은 'pushback'이다.
examples: I'm going to push back on the timeline. It's unrealistic.
Residents pushed back against the new parking rules.
She got a lot of pushback when she suggested cutting the budget.

similar.example: I take issue with how those numbers were presented.
Don't be afraid to challenge the assumption.

vocab.example: We need tangible results by the end of the quarter, not just promises.
The union won a few concessions on working hours.
What can we glean from the first week of sales?
She's unaffiliated, so she votes for whoever makes the best case.
The meeting was pro forma. Everyone knew the decision had already been made.
The CEO was grilled for six hours during his deposition.
The lawyer was hit with sanctions for ignoring the court's deadline.
They spliced two interviews together to make it sound like he said something he didn't.
The small shop couldn't survive the onslaught of cheap online competitors.

warmup.q: When a big news story is full of uncertainty, how do you usually follow it, and how do you decide what to believe?
warmup.hint_ko: 주로 보는 매체, 익명 취재원이나 속보를 대하는 태도, 확인 습관 등을 말해보기.

warmup.q: Have you ever had a plan called off at the last minute? What happened?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적 경험(출장, 여행, 행사)과 그때의 감정, 대처를 말하기. 'only to have...' 패턴 연습.

opinion.q: The episode warns that early-voting numbers are a poor predictor of results. Why do people still read so much into early data, and when is that risky?
opinion.hint_ko: 초기 데이터에 의미를 부여하는 심리, 선거 외 사례(초기 판매량, 설문 등), 표본 편향 위험 언급.

opinion.q: Oil prices jumped just on the talk of military action. How much do markets react to words versus actual events?
opinion.hint_ko: 기대와 심리가 가격에 미치는 영향, 헤드라인 변동성, 개인이나 기업의 대응 방식.

debate.q: Should a sitting president be treated like any other litigant and be forced to testify in a lawsuit he filed himself?
debate.for: 소송을 제기한 사람은 상대방의 증거 요구에 응해야 하고, 법 앞의 평등과 법치 원칙상 예외가 없어야 한다.
debate.against: 대통령 업무의 특수성과 국가 안보 일정을 고려해야 하며, 소송이 정치적 압박 수단으로 쓰일 수 있으므로 일정 조율 등 보호 장치가 필요하다.

debate.q: Is it better for a media company to settle with a powerful plaintiff or fight back in court?
debate.for: 합의하면 비용과 불확실성이 줄고 본업에 집중할 수 있다.
debate.against: 합의는 더 많은 소송을 부르는 선례가 되고, 끝까지 싸워야 언론 독립성과 신뢰를 지킬 수 있다.

roleplay.scenario: Your team's big product launch might be delayed because a key client keeps sending mixed signals. In a quick meeting, you and your colleague assess how likely the delay is and decide how to prepare.
roleplay.your_role: Project lead who has to explain the signs of a possible delay, push back on an unrealistic deadline, and propose a contingency plan.
roleplay.partner_role: Senior colleague who is skeptical, wants the launch to stay on schedule, and asks tough questions.
goals: Describe the evidence honestly, noting it points to a possibility but not a certainty.
Push back politely on the deadline using at least two expressions from the episode (e.g., 'push back', 'at its core', 'strain credulity').
Agree on a plan so the team doesn't end up with something called off at the last minute.

useful_phrases.phrase: This points to the growing possibility, but not the certainty, of...
useful_phrases.ko: ~의 가능성이 커지고 있지만 확정은 아니라는 뜻

useful_phrases.phrase: It's important not to over-interpret the data.
It's just impossible to predict if...
I do want to stress that...
Let's look at X again, where...
useful_phrases.ko: X를 다시 보자, 거기서는~ (사례로 넘어갈 때)

useful_phrases.phrase: We have zero way to tell whether...

shadowing.reason_ko: 불확실한 상황을 설명하는 전형적인 분석 화법이다. 'perhaps the only person who knows for sure', 'only to have it called off' 같은 패턴을 리듬 있게 따라 하기 좋다.
데이터를 해석할 때 단서를 달며 말하는 구조('It's important not to over-interpret... But...')를 익히기 좋다. 회의나 패널에서 바로 쓸 수 있다.
'you're also seeing others battle back', 'decide how willing he is to play by the rules'처럼 긴 문장을 연결하고 수사적 질문으로 끝내는 호흡을 연습하기 좋다.

difficulty.note_ko: 뉴스 브리핑 특유의 빠른 속도와 정치·법률 용어(deposition, discovery, sanctions)가 나온다. 문장 구조는 비교적 명료하고, 인터뷰 형식이라 구어 표현과 담화 표지를 익히기 좋다.

translations_sent.0-0: 미국이 세 번째 항공모함을 중동으로 보냅니다.
translations_sent.1-1: 이란에 대한 군사 공격 가능성을 시사하는 징후가 나오면서 유가가 다시 오르고 있습니다.
translations_sent.2-2: 또 한 차례의 전투로 무엇을 얻을 수 있을까요?
translations_sent.4-4: A 마르티네스였고요, NPR 뉴스의 UP FIRST입니다.
translations_sent.6-6: 주요 경합주의 투표율이 지난 중간선거와 비교해 크게 올랐습니다.
translations_sent.7-7: 이 데이터에서 우리는 무엇을 알 수 있을까요?
translations_sent.8-8: 그리고 트럼프 대통령은 BBC를 상대로 낸 100억 달러 규모의 명예훼손 소송에서 증언해야 합니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 판사는 소송을 하고 싶다면 법원의 규칙을 따라야 한다고 말했습니다.
translations_sent.10-10: BBC는 선서한 대통령에게 무엇을 물어볼 수 있을까요?
translations_sent.12-12: 하루를 시작하는 데 필요한 뉴스를 준비했습니다.
translations_sent.13-13: 앞으로 몇 주 안에 이란에서 더 격렬한 전투가 벌어질 가능성을 가리키는 구체적인 움직임들이 있습니다.
translations_sent.14-14: 군 증원 병력이 들어가고 있고, 일부 미국 인력은 이 지역에서 빠져나가고 있습니다.
translations_sent.15-15: 이 모든 걸 짚어보기 위해 NPR 국가안보 담당 기자 그렉 마이어 씨와 함께합니다.
translations_sent.16-16: 그렉, 어제 미국과 이스라엘이 대규모 공격을 감행할 수 있다는 잠재적 계획에 대해, 브리핑을 받은 한 인물이 익명을 조건으로 NPR에 말해 준 내용을 들었는데요.
translations_sent.18-18: 네, 몇 가지 단편적인 정보가 있습니다.
translations_sent.19-19: 하지만 앞으로 무슨 일이 벌어질지 확실히 아는 사람은 아마 트럼프 대통령뿐일 텐데, 그는 일부러 모호하게 말하고 있습니다.
translations_sent.20-20: 그리고 이번 전쟁에서 이미 봤듯이 트럼프는 자주 마음을 바꿉니다.
translations_sent.21-21: 미군이 어떤 작전을 준비해도 트럼프가 취소하고 다른 방향으로 가 버리는 경우가 있었습니다.
translations_sent.22-22: 우리가 확인한 건 공격 가능성에 대비한 준비 징후가 분명하다는 점입니다.
translations_sent.23-23: 미국이 세 번째 항공모함을 중동으로 보냅니다.
translations_sent.24-24: 피트 헤그세스 국방장관은 이번 주 이스라엘을 조용히 방문해 베냐민 네타냐후 총리를 만났습니다.
translations_sent.25-25: 미 국무부 직원 일부와 그 가족들이 사우디아라비아에서 철수하고 있습니다.
translations_sent.26-26: 그래서 종합하면, 확실하진 않지만 군사 행동 가능성이 커지고 있다는 뜻입니다.
translations_sent.28-28: 만약 군사 행동이 있다면 11월 3일 중간선거 전일까요, 후일까요?
translations_sent.29-29: 네, A, 선거 이후일 가능성이 훨씬 커 보입니다.
